paragraphs.dominant_move: metric selection -> standardization -> baseline top five -> 80 percent comparison
classification repair -> model II -> basketball, football, baseball, and women-coach lists -> claimed perfect fit
annual score plots -> bounded fluctuation -> slight upward trend
simpler calculation -> claimed accuracy and utility -> practical transfer
Sports Illustrated audience -> previous-century male-or-female coach decision -> four deliverables

global_organization_chain: The two-page summary moves from the coach-selection goal through the AHP-FCE baseline, the classified IAHP-FCE repair, cross-sport and gender applications, a cross-pool winner, time-line plots, four tests, and practical transfer claims.

The abstract compresses baseline construction and 80 percent fit, the two-level repair and claimed 100 percent fit, three-sport and women-coach lists, Pat Summitt, time-horizon behavior, testing, and broader-use claims.
The opening identifies Sports Illustrated and then restates four deliverables: choose coaches, test time horizon, transfer across gender and sport, and write a nontechnical article.
The literature review contrasts peer review, surveys, content analysis, and bibliometrics before selecting AHP and fuzzy comprehensive evaluation as complementary qualitative-quantitative methods.

The assumptions define the candidate pool, Internet-data trust, retained metrics, classification logic, and three first-level concepts, while the notation table binds sample size, weights, judgment matrix, dispersion, CIC, and score.

The data section chooses Internet collection, applies an approximately top-40 screening line per sport, displays sport-specific metric hierarchies, and passes nonnegative metric arrays to normalization.

The baseline model defines benefit, cost, and middle-type membership formulas, a fuzzy matrix, dispersion-driven pairwise judgments, reciprocal consistency conditions, a CIC correction program, and a weighted composite score.

The basketball test builds a 13-by-13 matrix, estimates weights in LINGO, reports CIC 0.032, ranks five coaches, rejects the list against external examples, and turns that failure into requirements for classification and simpler calculation.
The repair groups metrics into first-level classifications, calculates within-group weights, introduces classification weights, and aggregates local scores into the IAHP-FCE final score.
The basketball application fixes Experience, Achievement, and Competency, solves three local matrices, assigns top-level weights 0.35, 0.40, and 0.25, and produces an improved top-five list.
The football application reuses the interface with a sport-specific ten-metric structure, three local matrices, the same top-level weights, and a 76-coach ranking.
The paper falls back to the unclassified model for three baseball metrics and seven women-basketball metrics, producing two more top-five lists and claiming broad sport and gender applicability.
The decision section compares scores produced from different sport-specific metric systems and names Pat Summitt the overall winner before supplying a short biographical justification.
Annual composite-score tables and four coach plots compare gender and sport combinations, then infer bounded fluctuation with a slight upward career trend.
The testing section invokes dimension consistency, top-five membership overlap, assumption reasonableness, and a one-factor baseball rank-stability sweep before declaring the model qualified.
The audience article explains the less-than-ten versus more-than-nine branch, lists sport winners, dramatizes Pat Summitt, and translates the time-horizon claim into advice for coaches.

The final evaluation praises standardization, decomposition, metric quantification, classification, and universality, then identifies indicator burden and missing team-management data and proposes better collection and quantification.
The references identify method, sports, ranking, and sensitivity sources but do not freeze the input datasets, external rankings, spreadsheets, LINGO files, or MATLAB code used in the calculations.
Only after the positive language, organization, model, result, and visual chain is complete does the final pass record formula, matrix, inference, comparability, and reproducibility warnings.

main_argument_chains.claim: A coach-ranking baseline is inspectable when sport metrics pass through declared normalization, dispersion, judgment, consistency, and score equations.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Reuse the baseline only after repairing its endpoint scale and printed judgment/CIC defects.

main_argument_chains.claim: The model-II repair responds to an observed baseline failure by separating local metric weights from first-level class weights.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Keep the failure-to-repair logic, but document class-weight provenance and uncertainty.

main_argument_chains.claim: Cross-sport and gender applications demonstrate a reusable calculation interface only when each receiving roster and metric mapping remains explicit.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat each list as a scoped rerun rather than proof of universal sport or gender invariance.

main_argument_chains.claim: An overall best-coach decision requires a common score contract that the source's sport-specific systems do not establish.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Do not compare the displayed composite scores until measurement invariance or common-utility calibration is demonstrated.

main_argument_chains.claim: Time-horizon and sensitivity evidence is useful when annual observations, selection rules, perturbations, outputs, and uncertainty are all visible.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Replace anecdotal trend and rank-stability claims with population sampling, feasible perturbations, and uncertainty.

main_argument_chains.claim: The Sports Illustrated article preserves value when its plain-language branch and lists remain connected to validated analytical evidence.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Publish the audience artifact with corrected accuracy, comparability, validation, and reproducibility disclosures.

warnings.warning: Benefit and cost formulas divide by x_max+x_min and generally do not map observed extrema to the stated unit membership scale; verify the intended standardization before reuse.
The middle-optimum piecewise rule excludes x=x_max and lacks a complete endpoint and out-of-range contract.
The visual source prints an extra s(i)= inside the first b_ij branch and a dangling min after the b_m definition; reconstruct the intended rule before implementation.
The printed CIC objective compares y_ij with b_ji rather than b_ij; confirm whether the transpose is intentional before solving.
The sensitivity equations use r(i,j) for membership and r_j for perturbation without a clean symbol or feasibility contract, so the reported thresholds are not directly reusable.
